claims.text: Alloying a transition-metal catalyst with a second transition metal shifts its d-band center.
The d-band-center shift caused by alloying governs catalytic selectivity.
The d-band-center shift caused by alloying governs catalyst durability.
The effect of the d-band center on selectivity and durability is mediated by adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Cu alloying of Pt will shift the d-band center of the catalyst surface atoms.
A Pt-Cu composition series can be prepared under identical synthesis and heat-treatment conditions.
Holding the stated test conditions constant will ensure that observed performance changes arise primarily from alloying.
A d-band center closer to the Fermi level generally produces stronger adsorption.
Stronger adsorption can slow desorption and cause catalyst poisoning.
A more negative d-band center weakens adsorption.
Adsorption-strength changes caused by a d-band shift affect rate-determining reaction steps.
An appropriately shifted d-band center in Pt-Cu will decrease the adsorption strength of reactive intermediates relative to pure Pt.
Weaker intermediate adsorption in appropriately alloyed Pt-Cu will improve selectivity by favoring the desired reaction pathway.
Weaker intermediate adsorption in appropriately alloyed Pt-Cu will improve durability by reducing deactivation from strongly adsorbed species.
The proposed relationship should hold when reaction kinetics are governed by adsorbate binding energies.
The proposed relationship should hold only when alloying reliably shifts the d-band center and phase segregation or other structural changes do not dominate.
XPS or UPS can characterize the d-band-center shift in the Pt-Cu series.
A lack of correlation between measured d-band-center shifts, adsorption-energy proxies, and catalytic performance would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes cases in which alloying does not reliably shift the d-band center, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of Cu alloying to produce the expected shift as falsification. That result would instead be a failed intervention outside the stated applicability boundary.

The hypothesis states that the optimal d-band shift is unknown and predicts improvement only for an 'appropriately shifted' alloy, but the falsification rule treats failure of the tested Cu ratios to improve selectivity or durability as decisive without establishing that those ratios span the appropriate shift.
